topic_metadata.topic_title: Measurement and Dimensions of Physical Quantities

topics.core_competency: The learner uses a variety of instruments to accurately measure physical quantities and applies the concept of dimensions to establish the relation between these quantities.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: measure a variety of physical quantities in the environment with minimal errors. (v/a, s, gs)
analyse the dimensions of a variety of derived physical quantities and use them to check the consistency of equations. (v/a, u, s, gs)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners brainstorm the fundamental and derived physical quantities met in their previous studies and make presentations.
Learners review the concepts of scientific notation and significant figures (s.f) and make presentations.

Individually or collaboratively, learners measure a variety of physical quantities using appropriate instruments and state their accuracies (digital measuring instruments, vernier callipers and micrometre screw gauges should be emphasised), then they make presentations.
In groups, learners identify the sources of errors for a variety of measurements and devise means to minimise them during discussions.
Learners collaboratively establish the accuracy of calculated values in a variety of situations and make presentations.
Learners explain the meaning of the dimensions of a physical quantity in a class discussion.

Learners state the dimensions of the fundamental physical quantities and use them to determine the dimensions of different derived quantities like power, force, velocity, acceleration, momentum and others.
In groups, learners check the consistency of equations using dimensions and make presentations.
In groups, learners discuss the merits and demerits of dimensional analysis and report in plenary.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners as they brainstorm physical quantities, scientific notation and significant figures as you assess their interaction, how confidently they express their ideas and the correctness of the concepts
Probe learners on how to: i) determine and minimise errors in measurements; and ii) record measurements to a correct number of decimal places (d.p) and significant figures for different instruments.

Evaluate learners’ written work focussing on: i) the units and accuracies of measurements; ii) interconversion of units; iii) a written explanation of how errors are minimised; and iv) the accuracy of calculated values in line with d.p and s.f.

Observe learners in their discussion on dimensions of fundamental and derived physical quantities while assessing: i) confidence during the discussions; ii) use of ICTs in presentations where possible; and iii) respect for others’ views.
Converse with learners about how the different quantities are related using dimensional analysis. Ask probing questions to clear misconceptions.

Assess learners’ written work while looking for: i) their ability to check the consistency of equations using dimensions; and ii) the correctness of the statements for the merits and demerits of using dimensions.

practicals.title: Measurement of Physical Quantities
practicals.description_verbatim: Individually or collaboratively, learners measure a variety of physical quantities using appropriate instruments and state their accuracies (digital measuring instruments, vernier callipers and micrometre screw gauges should be emphasised)

suggested_uses: use of ICTs in presentations where possible

topics.core_competency: The learner investigates the effect of a number of forces on a system and how the centre of gravity relates to the stability of mechanical structures.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: determine the resultant of vectors in different situations. (v/a, u, s)
appreciate the concepts of moments and torque in the construction of different structures. (u, s, gs, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups or as individuals, learners review the meaning of scalar and vector quantities, and identify examples of each.
As individuals or groups, learners determine the resultant vector in different situations during class discussions.
Learners collaboratively review the terms; moment of a force, centre of gravity, couple, equilibrium, torque, and make presentations.
Learners carry out investigations to determine the moment of a couple, centre of gravity of different shapes and analyse the data.
Individually or in groups, learners describe how centre of gravity affects stability of structures and make presentations.
Learners perform tasks such as; determining the resultant force at the point where the ladder is in contact with the ground as shown in the figure below.
Learners carry out group project work for modelling structures (bridges, roofing systems etc) and make recommendations on safety precautions in plenary.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners’ presentations on determining the resultant of vectors while focusing on: i) individual learner’s skills to resolve vectors; ii) ability of learners to apply different methods to obtain resultant vectors; and iii) team building among learners.
Converse with learners about the different methods of obtaining the resultant vector while assessing whether they can compare the different methods.
Evaluate learners’ products in the form of write-ups about the resultant vector. Check for the use of equations, sketch diagrams and accuracy of responses.

Observe learners as they carry out investigations to determine the moment of a couple while assessing their ability to: i) plan; ii) use a variety of media/techniques to present findings; and iii) effectively express themselves during presentations.
Converse with learners while assessing how they organise investigations, record and analyse observations, and make conclusions.

Assess the written work by considering: i) accuracy of the meaning of the terms couple, torque and how they are related; ii) coherence in procedures for carrying out investigations and drawing conclusions; iii) relevancy in the application of the principle of moments on different force systems; iv) workability of the models in relation to the structures under investigation; and v) the ability of learners to solve related numerical problems by interpreting data and applying the correct equations.

practicals.title: Determination of Moment of a Couple and Centre of Gravity
practicals.description_verbatim: Learners carry out investigations to determine the moment of a couple, centre of gravity of different shapes and analyse the data.

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: Learners carry out group project work for modelling structures (bridges, roofing systems etc) and make recommendations on safety precautions in plenary.
project_requirements.deliverables_verbatim: Models of structures, recommendations on safety

topics.core_competency: The learner investigates the effect of force on the motion of bodies on land, water and air, and devises safety precautions for users of automobiles.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: derive the equations describing the linear motion of uniformly accelerated objects and apply them in a variety of situations. (u, s, gs)
determine the relative velocity and the distance of closest approach for moving bodies in real life. (u, s, gs)
verify the principle of conservation of linear momentum and apply it in a variety of situations. (u, s, gs)
apply Newton’s laws of motion in different situations. (u, s, gs)

explicitly_excluded.text_verbatim: Rigid bodies should be left out.

depth_limitations.text_verbatim: Emphasis should be put on linear motion only.

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners review and discuss the meanings of the terms; distance, displacement, speed, velocity, and acceleration as applied to uniform motion and represent them graphically.
Learners individually or in groups search and derive the equations of uniformly accelerated motion (for linear motion) and apply them to solve a variety of numerical problems.

In groups, learners investigate the concepts of relative velocity and closest distance of approach, and their application in real-life situations (such as crossing roads, rivers and aeroplane motion) and make presentations.
Learners individually or in groups apply concepts of relative motion to solve numerical problems.
Basing on prior knowledge, in groups learners brainstorm the meaning of linear momentum and its units.
In groups or individually, learners derive and state the principle of conservation of linear momentum and apply it to solve numerical problems in different scenarios of collisions.
In groups, learners use their prior knowledge to state Newton’s laws of motion and discuss their implications in real life.
In groups, learners derive the expression F = ma, and use it to determine the resultant force on objects.
Learners individually or in groups apply Newton’s laws to explain motion in lifts, connected particles and other real-life situations.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners during the discussion session while assessing whether they correctly explain the terminologies used under motion and their relationships. Also assess how learners: i) confidently express themselves; ii) respect others’ opinions; and iii) willingly and actively participate.
Converse with learners to probe their understanding of the interpretation of the graphs of motion in different situations.
Assess learners’ written products while looking for the logical flow of the methods of deriving the equations and their applications in solving numerical problems.
Observe learners while assessing their ability to: i) amicably build and work in teams; ii) confidently express themselves; and iii) respect others’ opinions during the presentations.
Discuss with learners while probing them on the correct use of direction, sketches and formulae for obtaining relative motion.
Assess learners’ written products while looking for accuracy in solving numerical problems related to relative motion.
Observe learners while assessing their ability to: i) amicably build and work in teams; ii) confidently express themselves; and iii) respect others’ opinions.
Evaluate learners’ ability to derive and apply expressions for linear momentum and energy under different collisions.
Converse with learners while assessing their ability to relate different types of collision to real-life experiences.
Assess the written products of learners while looking for accuracy of statements about momentum and in solving numerical problems.

Observe learners during the discussion session while assessing how they: i) effectively express themselves; ii) ask evaluative questions to further their understanding; and iii) accurately state Newton’s laws of motion.
Converse with learners about the implications of Newton’s laws while assessing their confidence and the correctness of the information.

Assess written products while looking for: i) how learners correctly apply Newton’s laws in calculations in different situations; and ii) the relevancy and coherency of the implications of Newton’s laws in everyday life.

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: Note: Rigid bodies should be left out. Emphasis should be put on linear motion only.

topics.core_competency: The learner investigates the effect of force on bodies moving under gravity and the applications of this phenomenon in different situations.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: analyse the behaviour of bodies moving under gravity. (u, s, gs)
derive the equations of projectile motion and apply them in different real-life situations. (v/a, u, s, gs)

explicitly_excluded.text_verbatim: Projectiles on inclined planes should be left out.

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners use prior knowledge to review the meaning of acceleration due to gravity and discuss its effect on moving objects.
In groups or as individuals, learners determine the value of acceleration due to gravity using different methods.
In groups, learners review the terminologies used in relation to projectile motion.
Learners investigate the motion of a projectile and determine the velocity, height, time of flight and range on a horizontal surface.
In groups, learners model systems that employ projectile motion (bouncing castles, bouncing balls and any other) and make demonstrations.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners during the discussion session while assessing how they: i) effectively express themselves; ii) ask evaluative questions to further their understanding; and iii) accurately define and explain the effect of acceleration due to gravity on bodies.
Assess learners’ ability to: i) design experiments for the determination of acceleration due to gravity; and ii) interpret, manipulate and analyse experimental data to make valid conclusions.

Observe learners during the discussion session about terms used under projectile motion and their applications while assessing the: i) Use of ICTs in communicating ideas where possible; ii) learners’ confidence; and iii) active participation during the discussion.
Converse with learners while looking for the appropriateness of the video/pictures based on applications of projectile motion.

Assess the product while looking for: i) the correct meaning of terminologies used; ii) the logical flow of derivations of equations under projectile motion; iii) correct substitutions when solving numerical problems; and iv) workability of the designed models.

practicals.title: Determination of Acceleration Due to Gravity
practicals.description_verbatim: In groups or as individuals, learners determine the value of acceleration due to gravity using different methods.

investigative_skills.text_verbatim: design experiments for the determination of acceleration due to gravity

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: In groups, learners model systems that employ projectile motion (bouncing castles, bouncing balls and any other) and make demonstrations.

suggested_uses: Use of ICTs in communicating ideas where possible

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: Note: Projectiles on inclined planes should be left out.

topics.core_competency: The learner investigates the resources and transformations of energy in the environment in order to ensure sustainable and improved efficiency of energy utilisation.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: derive expressions for work, power and energy, and apply them to solve real-life problems. (u, s, gs)
explain the work-energy theorem, conservative and non-conservative force fields and how they relate to different bodies. (u, s, gs)
describe the structure and the energy production process of the Sun and its implication to life on Earth. (u, v/a, gs)
apply the concepts of renewable and non-renewable energy resources in the conservation of energy. (u, s, gs, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners review and brainstorm the meaning of the terms—work, energy and power. Then they discuss the importance of energy conservation and make presentations.
In groups, learners derive the expressions; k.e = 1/2 mv^2, p.e = mgh, P = Fv and apply them to solve numerical problems.
Learners in groups, research, discuss and present the work-energy theorem and its practical applications.
Learners research and make presentations on conservative and non-conservative force fields and their applications in real life.
Learners collaboratively develop a model for the car crash experiment using trolleys, inclined planes, marbles and different masses.
Learners discuss how different speeds/velocities of automobiles relate to energy consumption/emission of greenhouse gases and environmental conservation.
In groups, learners search for and make presentations on: i) the composition and structure of the sun; ii) the process of energy production by the sun; and iii) harnessing solar energy.
Learners debate the merits and demerits of solar energy for the sustenance of life on Earth.

In groups, learners review and discuss how the sun is the primary source of the following renewable energies: i) hydro energy; ii) wind energy; iii) biomass energy; iv) geothermal energy; and v) tidal energy.
In groups, learners explore the operation of the following and make presentations: i) solar thermal technologies; ii) solar photovoltaic (PV) systems; and iii) thermal storage systems.
In class projects, learners model devices that harness solar energy such as solar collectors, cookers, dryers, heaters, storage systems and discuss their importance to the community.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners in the brainstorming session about the concepts of work, energy and power, and in the derivation of the expressions while assessing learners: i) active participation; ii) confidence in presentations; and iii) correctness of the information about the meaning of work, energy and power, and the importance of energy conservation.
Assess the written products by looking for: i) correct procedure of derivation; and ii) correct use of the equations in solving numerical problems.

Probe learners during the discussion to ascertain the: i) correctness of the statement of the work-energy theorem; ii) relevant applications of the theorem to solve problems; and iii) correct meaning of conservative and non-conservative force fields and how they help to explain natural phenomena like gravitational field, magnetic field, etc.

During the project, probe learners to ascertain how they: i) demonstrate understanding of the work-energy theorem; ii) identify the energy changes at each step of motion; iii) explain the effects of green-house gases on the environment; and iv) demonstrate an appreciation for energy conservation for the future.

Observe learners’ presentations and debate while assessing: i) the correctness of the information about the composition and structure of the Sun; ii) the accuracy of the information about how energy is produced by the Sun; iii) the correctness of how solar energy is harnessed by the community; iv) self-expression, confidence and respect for others’ opinions during the debate; and v) the learners’ products in terms of write-ups on the concepts of work, energy and power.
In a conversation, assess learners’ understanding of: i) different sources of energy; ii) the merits and demerits of different sources of energy; and iii) the solar thermal systems and photovoltaics.
Assess learners’ write-ups while looking for the correct meaning of sun intensity, operating temperatures, cell output current, shadow effect, climate effect and electrical load matching.

Assess the learners’ products while looking for: i) selection of materials for the models; ii) coherence and correctness of procedures in making models; iii) innovativeness and collaboration in the project work; and iv) workability and usefulness of the developed model to the community.

practicals.title: Car Crash Model Experiment
practicals.description_verbatim: Learners collaboratively develop a model for the car crash experiment using trolleys, inclined planes, marbles and different masses.

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: In class projects, learners model devices that harness solar energy such as solar collectors, cookers, dryers, heaters, storage systems and discuss their importance to the community.

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: Note: Safety precautions and environmental conservation should be taken into consideration.

topics.core_competency: The learner investigates factors that determine solid friction and its effect on static and dynamic systems, and uses this concept to model efficient systems with minimised friction.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: investigate the nature of friction between static bodies and its implications. (u, s, gs, v/a)
investigate the effects of friction on dynamic bodies in order to improve the operation of systems. (u, s, gs)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners individually or as groups investigate the nature of friction between static bodies and make models to demonstrate the molecular theory of solid friction.
Learners in groups carry out experiments to determine the coefficient of static friction.
In class discussions, learners solve numerical problems involving the coefficient of static friction.
Learners in groups or as individuals, determine experimentally the coefficients of dynamic friction for moving systems.
In class discussions, learners use the coefficient of dynamic friction in solving numerical problems.
Learners make models of braking systems of bicycles, motorcycle, cars, trucks and explain their operation in presentations.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners as they make the models demonstrating molecular theory while assessing their: i) active participation, creativity, collaboration and leadership; and ii) ability to explain their models in relation to the molecular theory of solid friction and the laws that govern it.
Assess the modelled products of learners while looking for creativity, innovation and workability.

Assess learners’ write-ups on (a) and (b) above while looking for coherence and correctness of procedures in experiments, making models and proper application of expressions in solving numerical problems.

Evaluate the experiments in terms of: i) correct selection and use of apparatus; ii) proper recording of results; iii) correct analysis of data; iv) identifying sources of errors; v) making appropriate conclusions; and vi) consideration of safety precautions.
Assess the correctness and coherence of the learners’ written work on experiments and the accuracy of the solutions to numerical problems.
Assess models in terms of learners’ creativity, innovation, effective communication and workability.

practicals.title: Determination of Coefficient of Static Friction
practicals.description_verbatim: Learners in groups carry out experiments to determine the coefficient of static friction.

practicals.title: Determination of Coefficient of Dynamic Friction
practicals.description_verbatim: Learners in groups or as individuals, determine experimentally the coefficients of dynamic friction for moving systems.

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: Learners make models of braking systems of bicycles, motorcycle, cars, trucks and explain their operation in presentations.

topics.core_competency: The learner investigates the effect of molecular forces in fluids, fluid pressure and their applications in fluid systems.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: examine molecular forces in liquids and their implications. (u, s, gs)
assess the application of pressure in fluids in different situations. (s, u)
explain pressure variations in flowing fluids and its applications in variety of situations. (u, s, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Using think-pair-share, learners review, discuss and make presentations on the occurrence of surface tension, capillarity and factors which affect them.

In groups, learners carry out activities to: i) determine coefficient of surface tension and measure angle of contact for liquids and their implications on liquids; ii) derive expressions describing surface tension, capillarity, excess pressure in bubbles, and surface energy; and iii) use derived expressions to solve numerical problems.
In pairs, learners research and make presentation on the effect of viscosity on the motion of bodies in fluids.

Learners review, brainstorm and present on the density of fluids, fluid pressure, Pascal’s principle, Archimedes’ principle, law of floatation, experiments to verify Archimedes’ principle, law of floatation and their implications and applications.
Learners in groups research and present the derivation of expressions for Archimedes’ principle, law of floatation and apply them to solve numerical problems.
Learners in groups model devices which apply Pascal’s principle.

Learners research, discuss and present on: i) the meaning of streamline and turbulent flow of fluids; ii) the derivation of the expression for the equation of continuity; iii) the statement of Bernoulli’s principle and derive its equation; iv) the applications of Bernoulli’s principle in a variety of situations; v) the derivation of Stokes’s and Poiseuille’s formulae and use them to solve numerical problems; vi) the measurement of the coefficient of viscosity; vii) the measurement of terminal velocity using different liquids; and viii) the explanation of the effect of temperature on viscosity of fluids using molecular theory.
Learners in groups model devices that apply Bernoulli’s principle in their operations.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners’ group discussions while looking for the correctness of the meaning of surface tension, capillarity and angle of contact with focus on learners’ confidence in expressing ideas, team building and respect for others’ views.

Converse with learners while assessing their ability to determine the coefficient of surface tension, measure the angle of contact, determine excess pressure in bubbles, surface energy, and the effect of viscosity on the motion of bodies in fluids.
Assess learners’ written work while looking for: i) coherence and accuracy in the procedures; ii) appropriateness of explanations; and iii) accuracy in solutions to solved numerical problems.
Observe learners’ participation in discussions and look out for the correctness of the terms, principles and laws, implications, and correct any misconceptions.
Dialogue with learners while assessing their ability to correctly: i) derive the expressions for Archimedes’ principle and law of floatation; and ii) use the expressions to solve numerical problems.
Assess learners’ products to check on: i) the appropriateness and correct use of the materials selected; and ii) creativity, critical thinking, and workability of the model designed.

Dialogue with learners while assessing the correctness of the: i) meaning of streamline and turbulent flow of fluids; ii) statement of Bernoulli’s principle; iii) derivation of the expressions for the equation of continuity and Bernoulli’s principle; iv) derivation of Stokes’ and Poiseuille’s formulae; v) use of expressions to solve numerical problems related to fluid flow; vi) procedures in the measurement of the coefficient of viscosity; and vii) explanation of the effect of temperature on viscosity of fluids using molecular theory.
Evaluate learners’ products while checking on the: i) appropriateness and the correct use of the materials selected; and ii) creativity, critical thinking, and workability of the model designed.

practicals.title: Determination of Coefficient of Surface Tension
practicals.description_verbatim: In groups, learners carry out activities to: i) determine coefficient of surface tension and measure angle of contact for liquids and their implications on liquids

practicals.title: Verification of Archimedes’ Principle
practicals.description_verbatim: experiments to verify Archimedes’ principle, law of floatation

practicals.title: Measurement of Coefficient of Viscosity
practicals.description_verbatim: measurement of the coefficient of viscosity

practicals.title: Measurement of Terminal Velocity
practicals.description_verbatim: measurement of terminal velocity using different liquids

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: Learners in groups model devices which apply Pascal’s principle.

topics.core_competency: The learner explores the effects of force on the strength of different materials in order to guide on the selection of appropriate materials for construction work.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: investigate the elastic and plastic behaviour of stretched materials and their implications. (s, gs)
investigate Young’s Modulus and the work done during elastic extension and compression process of elastic materials. (u, s, gs, v/a)

explicitly_excluded.text_verbatim: Bulk modulus and shear rigidity should be left out.

suggested_learning_activities.description: In a brainstorming session, learners review prior knowledge on terminologies related to mechanical properties of materials, sketch stress-strain curves and make presentations.
Learners review Hooke’s law, features of a stress- strain curve for ductile materials in series and parallel arrangement, and make presentation.
Learners demonstrate ductility, brittleness, stiffness and strength, stress, strain and work out numerical problems related to them.
In groups or individually, learners derive the expression for Young’s Modulus and measure Young’s Modulus for different materials.
Learners research and make presentations on the work done during the extension or compression process for different materials.
In groups, learners model structures and explain their choice of materials based on the mechanical properties and exhibit their work.
In groups or individually, learners use derived expressions for Young’s Modulus to solve numerical problems.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe the learners’ participation during the brainstorming session while looking for: i) precise explanations of terms and laws; ii) ability of learners to categorise materials according to their mechanical properties; and iii) accuracy in sketching stress-strain curves.
Assess the accuracy of the learner’s written products about the investigation and the solutions to numerical problems.

Dialogue with learners to assess their understanding of the: i) physical quantities used in deriving the expression for Young’s Modulus; and ii) explanations of the shapes of stress-strain or load-extension graphs for different materials such as glass, rubber, copper and others.
Check how learners establish the relationship between elastic potential energy and stretching force, and apply it to solve numerical problems.
Assess the workability, innovation and originality of the model.

practicals.title: Measurement of Young's Modulus
practicals.description_verbatim: measure Young’s Modulus for different materials.

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: In groups, learners model structures and explain their choice of materials based on the mechanical properties and exhibit their work.

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: Note: Bulk modulus and shear rigidity should be left out.

topics.core_competency: The learner investigates the mode of operation of different types of thermometers and their applications in the real world.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: relate the expressions of temperature scales in order to solve real-life problems. (k, s, gs, v/a)
compare different types of thermometers and how they are used in real life. (u, s, gs, v/a)

explicitly_excluded.text_verbatim: Total radiation Pyrometer should not be considered.

suggested_learning_activities.description: In a brainstorming session, learners review terms and concepts such as thermometric properties, fixed points, absolute zero, temperature scales, and make presentations.
In groups or individually, learners derive expressions for different temperature scales, their interrelations and use them to solve numerical problems.

Learners research, discuss and report about the operations of different thermometers (constant volume gas thermometers, electrical resistance thermometers, digital infra-red thermometers, thermoelectric thermometer, optical pyrometer.
In groups, learners model different types of thermometers from locally available materials and use them to measure temperature.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Assess learners’ responses during the brainstorming session with respect to: i) correctness of concepts; and ii) effective self-expression.

Assess learners’ products in line with the: i) accuracy and coherence in the derivation of the expressions of different temperature scales and their interrelations; and ii) ability to solve numerical problems related to temperature scales.
Assess learners’ written reports while looking for: i) correctness of the explanation on the operation of different thermometers; and ii) correct use and accuracy in measurement of temperature.
Assess: i) learners’ ability to collaborate and apply creativity in development of the model thermometers; and ii) the workability and creativity of the model thermometer.

practicals.title: Model Thermometer Construction
practicals.description_verbatim: In groups, learners model different types of thermometers from locally available materials and use them to measure temperature.

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: In groups, learners model different types of thermometers from locally available materials and use them to measure temperature.

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: Note: Total radiation Pyrometer should not be considered.

topics.core_competency: The learner explores the behaviour of substances when heat is applied to them in order to sustainably apply them in heat systems.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: deduce that different objects require different amounts of heat to change their temperatures. (u, gs, s, v/a)
evaluate the concept of change of state and its implication in real life. (u, s, gs)

explicitly_excluded.text_verbatim: Verification of Newton’s law of cooling and cooling correction should not be considered

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners in groups review, brainstorm and report about the: i) meaning of heat capacity and specific heat capacity (SHC); and ii) measurement of SHC by the method of mixtures.

In groups, learners: i) determine the SHC of solids and liquids using the electrical method; ii) determine the SHC of liquids using continuous flow method and suggest how errors are minimised; and iii) solve numerical problems related to SHC and make presentations.
Learners work in groups to research and make presentations on Newton’s law of cooling and the factors that affect the rate of cooling.

In groups, learners review in class discussions and report on the: i) the meaning of latent heat; ii) experimental determination of latent heat by method of mixtures; and iii) explanation of latent heat in terms of the molecular theory.

In groups, learners: i) determine the latent heat of Vaporisation and Fusion of water by electrical method; ii) discuss in a plenary, the sources of errors in a plenary; and iii) solve related numerical problems.

Learners work in groups to model systems that use the concepts of heat capacity and latent heat to improve energy conservation such as building materials, automobiles, cooking stoves, electric devices and any other suitable.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners’ contributions during the brainstorming while looking for the correctness of the definitions, formulae, units and coherence of the procedures for the method of mixtures.
Dialogue with learners while assessing the: i) coherence of the experimental procedures for electrical and the continuous flow methods; and ii) ability to compare the two methods used above.
Assess learners’ written products while looking for: i) coherence and correctness of experimental procedures; and ii) correct use of equations in solving numerical problems related to SHC.
Observe learners’ presentations while looking for correctness of the meanings, formulae, units and coherence of the procedures for the method of mixtures.
Dialogue with learners while assessing the: i) coherence of the experimental procedures for the electrical method; and ii) possible sources of errors and how they can be reduced.

Assess learner’s written product while looking for: i) coherence and correctness of experimental procedures; ii) use of equations in solving numerical problems related to latent heat; iii) appropriateness and assembling of the materials used for modelling; and iv) workability and applicability of the models.

practicals.title: Determination of Specific Heat Capacity
practicals.description_verbatim: In groups, learners: i) determine the SHC of solids and liquids using the electrical method; ii) determine the SHC of liquids using continuous flow method

practicals.title: Determination of Latent Heat
practicals.description_verbatim: In groups, learners: i) determine the latent heat of Vaporisation and Fusion of water by electrical method

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: Learners work in groups to model systems that use the concepts of heat capacity and latent heat to improve energy conservation such as building materials, automobiles, cooking stoves, electric devices and any other suitable.

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: Note: Verification of Newton’s law of cooling and cooling correction should not be considered

topics.core_competency: The learner investigates modes of heat transfer in nature and their application in industry and society.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: explain the mechanism of heat conduction in solids and how it applies to materials in heat systems. (u, gs, v/a)
examine the significance of convection in explaining weather and climate. (u, gs, v/a)
deduce that heat can be transferred in form of electromagnetic radiations and this has many real-life applications. (s, gs, v, a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners brainstorm the meaning of the concepts of heat conduction, the mechanism of heat conduction, the factors which affect the rate of heat conduction in a material and make presentations.
In groups, learners investigate and make presentations on the thermal conductivity of different materials and their applications in real life.
In class discussions, learners work out numerical problems related to thermal conductivity.
In a brainstorming session, learners review the meaning of convection and how it can be demonstrated in liquids and gases and its application.
Learners debate the implications of natural convection in relation to ocean currents, weather patterns and seasons.
Individually, learners review and discuss various ways of detecting thermal radiation and state properties of good and bad radiators /absorbers in plenary.
Learners in groups research on the meaning of black body radiation, its laws and use them to estimate the temperature of the Sun and other black bodies and make presentations.
In small groups, learners discuss the applications of black body radiation.
In class projects, learners model devices that employ heat transfer mechanisms.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners’ presentations while looking for: i) the correctness of the definitions, factors that affect heat transfer and the mechanism of heat transfer; and ii) participation and respect for others’ opinions.

Converse with learners while assessing the: i) coherence of the experimental procedures for the determination of the thermal conductivity of different materials; and ii) ability to explain applications of materials in relation to their thermal conductivities.
Assess learners’ written products while considering their ability to solve numerical problems related to thermal conductivity.

Observe learners’ during the brainstorming session while looking for: i) correctness of the meanings and explanations on the occurrence of convection in liquids and gases and applications; and ii) involvement and respect for others’ opinions.
Converse with learners while assessing the coherence and accuracy of the implications of convection in daily life.
Observe learners during the review while looking for: i) participation; and ii) respect for other peoples’ opinions.

Converse with learners while assessing the: i) correct illustration of the devices used for detection of thermal radiation and their mode of operation; ii) correct responses on the properties of good and bad radiators; iii) appropriate explanation of the concept of black body radiation with respect to heat absorption and radiation; and iv) correct statement and application of laws governing black body radiation.

Assess written products while looking for: i) correct explanation of black body radiation; ii) correct statements of the laws and their applications; iii) materials used in the models; iv) learners’ ability to collaborate and apply creativity in the development of the models; v) workability of the models; and vi) correct description of the applications of black body radiation.

practicals.title: Investigation of Thermal Conductivity
practicals.description_verbatim: In groups, learners investigate and make presentations on the thermal conductivity of different materials and their applications in real life.

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: In class projects, learners model devices that employ heat transfer mechanisms.

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: Note: Exclude Provost’s theory of exchanges.

topics.core_competency: The learner investigates the effect of heat on the properties of gases and their applications in the operation of different systems in the oil and gas industry.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: analyse the behaviour of ideal gasses under different conditions. (u, s, gs)
evaluate the kinetic theory of gases and use it to derive the expression for the pressure exerted by the gas. (s, u, gs)
modify the ideal gas equation to suit the behaviour of real gases. (u)
infer that vapours exert pressure and that this has many real-life applications. (u, s, gs, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners in groups investigate the effect of changing temperature, pressure and volume of ideal gases, deduce and verify the ideal gas laws and make presentations.
In class discussions, learners derive the ideal gas equation and other related expressions and apply them to solve a variety of numerical problems.
Learners use the concept of ideal gases to model systems that employ gas behaviour under different conditions.
Learners research about the kinetic theory of gases and discuss why a gas exerts pressure. Then they present in plenary.
Learners in a class discussion derive the expression P = 1/3 ρc^2 and state the assumptions made.

In groups, learners analyse the expression P = 1/3 ρc^2 and apply it to: i) deduce how the kinetic energy of the gases is dependent on their temperature of the gas; ii) deduce ideal gas laws; iii) verify Avogadro’s law, Dalton’s law of partial pressure and Grahams law of diffusion; and iv) solve related numerical problems related to them.

In groups, learners: i) discuss conditions under which real gases approximate ideal gas behaviour; ii) deduce the modifications required in the ideal gas equation to suit the behaviour of real gases; and iii) describe the key features of the P-V curves for real gases and discuss the significance of critical temperature to distinguish gases from vapours.

In groups, learners brainstorm and review the terminologies related to vapours; saturated vapour (SV), unsaturated vapour (USV) and saturated vapour pressure (SVP), and their applications to real life.

Learners in groups: i) investigate the variation of SVP of water with temperature and the implication of the results to water systems; ii) sketch the P-V graphs showing the variation of SVP, USVP with temperature and volume; and iii) distinguish between SV and USV and use the concept in solving related numerical problems.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners as they Investigate the effect of increasing and decreasing temperature, pressure and volume on an enclosed gas system while looking for their collaboration and active participation.
Converse with learners as they verify the gas laws focusing on correctness and coherence.

Assess learners’ written products in terms of: i) correct statement of ideal gas laws and their applications; ii) appropriateness of material selection and use in the models; iii) their ability to collaborate and apply creativity in the development of the models; and iv) workability of the model.

Observe learners as they discuss looking for the accuracy of the: i) procedure of the derivation; ii) application of the equation in estimating the pressure of an enclosed system; and iii) cooperation and respect for others’ opinions.
Converse with learners to check the: i) correctness of the assumptions made in ideal gas laws; and ii) coherence in the derivation of expressions for ideal gases.

Assess learners written products while looking for: i) the correctness of statement of assumptions and derivation of expressions; and ii) correct use of expressions to solve related numerical problems.
Assess learners’ derivations while looking for correct procedure of derivation, the assumptions made and modification.

Discuss with learners while looking for: i) correct properties of real gases; ii) modifications required to approximate ideal gases to real gases; iii) significance of Van der Waal’s equation; and iv) P-V graph for real gases and its features.
Assess learners written products on (b) above while looking for correctness of statements and expressions.
Observe learners as they brainstorm and carry out investigations while looking for teamwork, involvement and respect for others’ opinions.
Discuss with learners while checking for correctness of the terms, p-v graphs, implications and investigation procedures.

Assess learners’ written products on the correctness of: i) terminologies; ii) P-V graphs; iii) coherence of experimental procedures; and iv) use of expressions to solve numerical problems on vapours.

practicals.title: Investigation of Ideal Gas Laws
practicals.description_verbatim: Learners in groups investigate the effect of changing temperature, pressure and volume of ideal gases, deduce and verify the ideal gas laws and make presentations.

practicals.title: Variation of SVP with Temperature
practicals.description_verbatim: investigate the variation of SVP of water with temperature and the implication of the results to water systems

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: Learners use the concept of ideal gases to model systems that employ gas behaviour under different conditions.

topics.core_competency: The learner appreciates the behaviour of compressed gas systems in relation to their domestic and industrial applications.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: deduce that every system has internal energy which is a function of its temperature. (u, s)
analyse the first law of thermodynamics and its implications in real-life situations. (u, s, gs)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups or as individuals, learners: i) explain the terminologies related to thermodynamic processes and how they apply to real-life situations; ii) research about the concepts of external heat, internal energy and work done by an ideal gas; and iii) derive the expression for work done by a gas: W = Integral(PdV) and relate it to the compression of gas systems.

Learners in groups research, discuss and make presentations about: i) the molar heat capacities (Cp and Cv), molar ratio (gamma) of an ideal gas and ii) the first law of thermodynamics to deduce the expression dQ = dU + PdV.

In groups or as individuals, learners derive and make presentations on the relationship Cp - Cv = R and other expressions for isothermal and adiabatic processes and use them to solve a variety of numerical problems.

Learners discuss the concept of work done by an ideal gas at constant volume and constant pressure in relation to gas filling processes (gas cooker, compressors for refrigerators and air conditioners, washing machines, welding gas cylinders etc.).
Learners model the devices mentioned in (c) above where possible, and make exhibitions.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Converse with learners while looking for the correctness of the concepts of: i) external heat, internal energy and work done by an ideal gas; and ii) isothermal, isovolumetric and isobaric and adiabatic changes/processes.
Assess learners’ written product on the coherence of the procedures in the derivation of the expression for work done by an ideal gas and use it to solve numerical problem.

Observe learners’ presentations on derivations while looking for: i) correct procedure of derivation and the assumptions made; ii) correct use of the equations in solving numerical problems about thermodynamic processes; and iii) the correctness of the implications of the thermodynamic expressions and processes in real life.
Evaluate learners’ written products while looking for the coherence of the procedures in the derivation of thermodynamic expressions and their use in solving related numerical problems.

Assess learners’ modelled products in terms of: i) appropriateness of material selection and their use in the models; ii) their ability to collaborate and apply creativity in the development of the models; and iii) workability of the models.

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: Learners model the devices mentioned in (c) above where possible, and make exhibitions.

topics.core_competency: The learner investigates the light reflecting properties of different surfaces and their applications in real life.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: employ the laws of reflection of light at plane surfaces to resolve different life scenarios. (u, v/a)
apply curved reflecting surfaces in real-life situations. (u, gs, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners review, brainstorm and make presentations about the rectilinear propagation of light, the reversibility of light, statements and verification of the laws of reflection of light.

In groups or as individuals, learners research, discuss and derive the relationship between: i) angle of deviation and glancing angle for two plane mirrors inclined at an angle to each other; and ii) angle of rotation of a plane mirror and angle of rotation of the reflected ray and its real-life applications.
In groups, learners model optical systems that apply the laws of reflection of light at plane surfaces.
In groups, learners review, brainstorm and make presentations about terms used under curved mirrors and ray diagrams.
In groups, learners research, discuss and make presentations about mirror equations, magnification formula, and the relationship r = 2f for spherical mirrors.
In pairs, learners design experiments to measure the focal length of curved mirrors. They discuss and report on the sources of errors and how they can be minimised.
In groups, learners model simple devices that use curved mirrors including those used to harness solar energy for domestic use and in telecommunication systems.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners’ participation in the group work while looking for: i) accuracy of information; and ii) any misconceptions that need to be corrected.
Converse with learners about correctness and accuracy in the expressions derived.

Assess learners’: i) written products on the coherence of the procedures in the derivation of the expressions; ii) material selection for models and workability; and iii) ability to solve numerical problems about reflection on plane surfaces.
Listen to the group discussions while assessing the correctness of the: i) meaning of terms used in relation to curved mirrors; ii) procedures of derivations; and iii) use of ray diagrams.

Assess the experimental design based on the: i) correct use and choice of the mirrors; ii) accuracy and analysis of data collected; iii) conclusions drawn; iv) sources of errors and how they can be minimised; and v) participation and cooperation among the learners.
Assess learners’ products based on the correctness of their write-ups: i) in (b) above; and ii) on applications of curved reflecting surfaces.

practicals.title: Measurement of Focal Length of Curved Mirrors
practicals.description_verbatim: In pairs, learners design experiments to measure the focal length of curved mirrors.

investigative_skills.text_verbatim: design experiments to measure the focal length of curved mirrors

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: In groups, learners model simple devices that use curved mirrors including those used to harness solar energy for domestic use and in telecommunication systems.

topics.core_competency: The learner explores the refractive properties of different materials for application in industries and medicine.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: apply the concept of refraction on plane surfaces to various situations in real life. (u, gs, v/a)
analyse the concepts of critical angle and total internal reflection and their implications. (u, v/a, s, gs)
apply lenses in solving a variety of problems in the community. (u, gs, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners review, brainstorm and present on the concept of refraction on plane surfaces (liquids, glass blocks, semi-circular glass and prisms), its effects and the laws of refraction of light.

In groups, learners research, discuss and make presentations about: i) application of Snell’s law to derive the expression nsin(i) = constant for different media and use it to solve numerical problems; and ii) expressions that describe refraction of light by glass blocks and glass prisms.

Learners investigate the: i) refracting angle A, and minimum deviation Dmin for prisms; ii) refractive indices of different materials using various methods such as (small quantity of a transparent liquid on a concave mirror, real and apparent depth); and iii) sources of errors in determining the refractive indices and how they can be minimised.
Learners in groups review and present on the concepts of critical angle and total internal reflection, and their applications.

In groups or as individuals, learners: i) derive expressions relating critical angle and refractive index; ii) carry out an investigation to determine the refractive index of a liquid using air- cell method; and iii) solve numerical problems on critical angle and total internal reflection.
In a brainstorming session, learners review the terminologies related to thin lenses and make presentations.

In pairs or as individuals, learners research and make presentations about the: i) derivation of lens formula (convex and concave); ii) determination of focal lengths of lenses using various methods and evaluate the effectiveness of the methods used; iii) meaning of conjugate points, the lens maker’s formula and derive the expressions; and iv) meaning of spherical and chromatic aberrations, and how they can be minimised.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners’ participation while looking for the accuracy of the information and correct any misconceptions.

Dialogue with learners while assessing: i) the correctness in the statement of laws of refraction and application of the concept in real life; ii) coherence in the derivation of the expressions; iii) their ability to design investigations to determine the refracting angle A, the angle of minimum deviation, Dmin of a glass prism and refractive indices of different materials using various methods; and iv) their ability to solve numerical problems under refraction.
Assess learners’ products based on their write-ups in (b) above and the accuracy in the numerical problems solved.
Observe learners’ discussion while assessing the correctness of the concepts of critical angle, total internal reflection and their applications.

Dialogue with learners while assessing: i) coherence in the derivation of the expressions relating critical angle and refractive index; ii) their ability to perform the experiment to determine the refractive index of a liquid by air-cell method; and iii) their ability to solve numerical problems on critical angle and total internal reflection.
Assess learners’ written products to check whether they can write coherent derivations, experimental procedures and solve numerical problems related to critical angle and total internal reflection.
Listen to learners’ views while asking probing questions to assess the correct use of terms under lenses, fluency in expressions, involvement in discussions and critical thinking abilities.

During discussions, ask learners probing questions to assess their ability to: i) coherently follow the procedures to derive different expressions under thin lenses and in performing the experiment; ii) apply derived expressions to solve related numerical problems; and iii) explain the meaning of conjugate points and aberrations as applied to thin lenses.
Evaluate the quality of learning through assessment of learners’ products, their presentations and write-ups in the derivation of the lens formula.

practicals.title: Investigation of Refractive Indices
practicals.description_verbatim: Learners investigate the: i) refracting angle A, and minimum deviation Dmin for prisms; ii) refractive indices of different materials using various methods such as (small quantity of a transparent liquid on a concave mirror, real and apparent depth)

practicals.title: Determination of Refractive Index by Air-Cell Method
practicals.description_verbatim: carry out an investigation to determine the refractive index of a liquid using air- cell method

practicals.title: Determination of Focal Lengths of Lenses
practicals.description_verbatim: determination of focal lengths of lenses using various methods

investigative_skills.text_verbatim: design investigations to determine the refracting angle A, the angle of minimum deviation, Dmin of a glass prism and refractive indices of different materials using various methods

topics.core_competency: The learner explores the optical operation of different optical instruments that can be applied in a variety of fields such as medicine, military and navigation.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: explain the principle of operation of a compound microscope and their real-life applications. (u, s)
describe the principle of operation of refracting telescopes and their applications. (u, s)

explicitly_excluded.text_verbatim: The operation of reflecting telescopes should be left out.

depth_limitations.text_verbatim: Only compound microscopes and refracting telescopes should be considered.

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners research, discuss and make presentations on the following concepts; near point, far point, accommodation, visual angle, exit pupil (eye ring) and magnifying power of an optical instrument.

In pairs, learners research and discuss the principle of operation of a compound microscope, derive expressions for its magnification in normal and abnormal adjustments and their real-life applications.

Learners research, discuss and make presentations in groups on: i) the mode of operation of refracting telescopes; ii) derivations for the expressions of magnifications with the final image at near point, and at infinity; and iii) real-life applications of refracting telescopes.
In groups, learners carry out a project to model optical devices such as telescopes.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: discuss with learners during their presentations while looking for: i) the correct meaning of near point, far point, visual angle, eye ring and magnifying power; and ii) their ability to describe the principle of operation of a compound microscope in normal and abnormal adjustment.
Assess products to ensure that learners have coherent and accurate write-ups on the operation of a compound microscope, derivations of magnifications and applications in solving numerical problems.

Observe learners’ discussions, while looking for: i) accurate information on the mode of operation of refracting telescopes and correcting any misconceptions; and ii) accurate use of ray diagrams to form final images.
Assess learners’ product to check on: i) appropriateness and the use of the materials selected; ii) creativity and critical thinking; and iii) workability of the models.

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: In groups, learners carry out a project to model optical devices such as telescopes.

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: NOTE: Only compound microscopes and refracting telescopes should be considered. The operation of reflecting telescopes should be left out.

topics.core_competency: The learner investigates the behaviour of charges at rest and their applications in printing and energy storage in batteries.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: apply the concept of Electrostatics in production of charge in real-life situations. (u, s, gs)
appreciate the existence of a force between charges and its implications. (u, s, gs)
examine electric fields and their implications in various situations. (u, s)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In pairs, learners review, discuss and make presentations on: i) production and detection of charges by different methods; ii) distribution of charge on conductors of different shapes; and iii) corona discharge and its applications in real life.
In pairs, learners research and make presentations on the principle of Faraday’s ice pail experiment and its applications.
In groups, learners model and explain the operation of devices which include among others car sprayer, ink-jet printers, electrostatic air cleaners and the Van der Graaf generator.
In groups or individually, learners demonstrate the existence of force between charged bodies.
In groups, learners search for and make presentations on the expression of Coulomb’s law, and its applications in solving numerical problems.

Learners, in groups research, discuss and make presentations on: i) the interaction of electric fields around different charges; ii) the derivation of the expressions for resultant electric field intensity (E), electric field potential (V), work done and their applications in solving real-life problems; and iii) variation of E and V with the distance r from a charged body.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe and listen to the learners’ participation in a discussion while looking for accuracy of information and correct any misconceptions.
Assess the: i) choice of the materials used; ii) procedure used in the description of ice pail experiment; and iii) conclusions made based on charge distribution.

Assess learners’ product to check on: i) correctness of their write-ups on the experiments and models; ii) appropriateness and the use of the materials selected for the model; and iii) innovativeness and workability of the model designed.

Observe learners as they demonstrate the existence of force between two charged bodies while looking for: i) their participation, creativity and correctness; ii) appropriate choice of materials; and iii) critical thinking and respect for others’ opinions.
Assess learners write-ups while looking for: i) coherence and correctness in the statement and expression of Coulomb’s law; and ii) accuracy in solving numerical problems.

Engage with learners in their discussions while looking for correct: i) illustration of electric field patterns around charges; and ii) procedures in the derivation of expressions for resultant electric field, electric potential, work done, and their applications in solving related numerical problems.
Assess learners write-ups on (a) above while looking for accuracy and relevancy of applications.

practicals.title: Demonstration of Force Between Charged Bodies
practicals.description_verbatim: In groups or individually, learners demonstrate the existence of force between charged bodies.

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: In groups, learners model and explain the operation of devices which include among others car sprayer, ink-jet printers, electrostatic air cleaners and the Van der Graaf generator.

topics.core_competency: The learner models capacitors for use in electronic devices.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: appreciate that capacitors store charge and have many applications. (s, u)
apply the charging and discharging processes of a capacitor in electrical and electronic devices. (u, s, gs, a/v)
deduce that capacitors store energy which can be used in a variety of real-life situations. (u, s, gs)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups or as individuals, learners research and make presentations about: i) terminologies used in relation to capacitors; ii) factors affecting the capacitance parallel plate capacitor; iii) derivation of the expressions for the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor; iv) derivation of the expressions for effective capacitance in series and parallel networks; and v) application of expressions to solve numerical problems.
In pairs, learners model simple capacitors using local materials and apply them in making electrical devices.

Learners in groups research, discuss and make presentations on: i) charging and discharging processes of a capacitor; ii) sketch graphs on variation of p.d versus time for the charging and discharging processes and their explanations; and iii) description of the application of charging and discharging processes of capacitors.

Learners discuss the application of capacitors in; charge storage, tuning radio frequencies, smoothing of rectified a.c, loudspeakers, microphones, radios, sensors, power regulation, plastic films and others.

Learners research and make presentations on: i) source of energy stored on capacitors; ii) derivation of expressions for the energy stored on a charged capacitor and their use in solving numerical problems; and iii) the energy losses when isolated parallel plate capacitors are connected together.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Converse with learners during their presentations while looking for the: i) correct meaning of terms and description of factors affecting capacitance; ii) coherence of procedures in the derivation of expressions; and iii) accuracy of solving numerical problems.

Assess learners’ products while looking for: i) coherence in the description and correctness of numerical problems solved; and ii) choice of materials used in making a capacitor, innovativeness and workability of the model.

Discuss with learners in their discussions while looking for correctness: i) in the explanation of charging and discharging processes of a capacitor; ii) of sketch graphs on variation of p.d versus time for the charging and discharging processes and their explanations; and iii) of different applications of capacitors.
Assess learners’ products on the coherence and quality of write-ups in (a) above

Observe and listen to learners’ participation in a discussion while looking for: i) correctness of information and correct any misconceptions; ii) logical flow in the derivation of the expressions for energy; and iii) use of the derived expressions to solve related numerical problems.
Assess learners’ products on the coherence and quality of write-ups in (a) above.

practicals.title: Model Capacitor Construction
practicals.description_verbatim: In pairs, learners model simple capacitors using local materials and apply them in making electrical devices.

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: In pairs, learners model simple capacitors using local materials and apply them in making electrical devices.

topics.core_competency: The learner models electronic circuits using semiconductor materials and electronic devices for a variety of purposes.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: examine the performance of semiconductor diodes in different devices. (u, s, gs)
analyse the operation and application of transistors in various situations. (u, s, gs)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners review, brainstorm, discuss and make presentations on: i) number base systems; ii) logic gates and truth tables, and their applications; iii) bistable switches; and iv) potential dividers.

Learners research, discuss and make presentations on: i) conductors, insulators and semi-conductors in terms of energy band gaps; ii) doping process and formation of n-type, p-type semiconductors; and iii) the operation of p-n junction diodes and characteristics of diodes.
Learners in pairs use ICT tools to obtain simulations/animations videos on the operations and applications of junction diodes.

Learners are guided to research and make presentations about the: i) operation of n-p-n and p-n-p type transistors; ii) explanation of I-V characteristics for the transistors; and iii) uses of transistors as switches, and amplifiers in electronic devices.
In groups, learners derive expressions on the operations of transistors and use them to solve numerical problems.
In groups, learners model devices that employ diodes and transistors and describe how they work.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe and listen to the learners’ presentations in a discussion while looking for: i) accuracy of information and correct any misconceptions; ii) collaboration and teamwork; and iii) creativity and innovation in the use of ICT on simulation videos.

Converse with learners during their presentations while looking for: i) the correctness of the explanations and the meaning of conductors, insulators and semiconductors in terms of energy band gaps; ii) ability to suggest materials for doping to create n-type or p-type semiconductors; and iii) ability to explain the operation of a junction diode.
Evaluate learning by assessing the products focusing on the coherence of write-ups.

Assess the presentations of learners based on their ability to: i) distinguish between the operations of p-n-p and n-p-n transistors; ii) explain the applications of transistors in electronic circuits; iii) draw and interpret the I-V curves for transistors; and iv) correctly derive expressions on the operations of transistors and use them in solving numerical problems.
Assess learners’ products such as the workability of the devices modelled and innovations therein.

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: In groups, learners model devices that employ diodes and transistors and describe how they work.

suggested_uses: use ICT tools to obtain simulations/animations videos on the operations and applications of junction diodes
